messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 44
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Chef
- Trauma Type: Refugee
- Pcl5: 42

A few months after he turned thirty-two, Rajesh was living in a small city in northern India, working as a line cook in a hotel kitchen. He was good with his hands, fast with a knife, and he could read a busy service like a conductor reads an orchestra. His mother had died a few years before, and his father had passed when he was a boy, but he had a close circle of friends and a younger sister, Priya, who was married and lived nearby. He was not a political man. He did not attend rallies, and he did not post opinions on the internet. He just wanted to work, save money, and maybe one day open his own small dhaba-style restaurant.

The trouble started with a rumor. Someone in the neighborhood said Rajesh had been seen talking to a man from a different religious community. The rumor grew legs. A group of men came to his apartment one evening, not to ask questions, but to deliver a warning. Rajesh was slapped, kicked, and told to leave the city by the end of the week. He did not argue. He packed a single bag, withdrew his savings, and went to Priya’s house to say goodbye. She was terrified. She begged him to go, to get to a safe country, to not look back. He promised he would send for her when he could. That was twelve years ago.

The journey took eight months. Rajesh does not like to talk about the details, but the outlines are clear enough. He paid a smuggler. He walked through forests, rode in the back of trucks with strangers, slept in crowded safe houses where no one spoke. He was robbed twice. He was detained for three weeks in a concrete room with no window, where a man with a stick asked him questions he could not answer. He learned to keep his eyes down, to not ask for anything, to eat whatever was placed in front of him without tasting it. When he finally crossed the border into a country that would accept his claim, he was forty pounds lighter and had not spoken a full sentence in six weeks.

Now, at forty-four, Rajesh is the head chef at a busy South Asian fusion restaurant in a mid-sized Canadian city. He is respected by his staff. His biryani is famous. But in the kitchen, he is always watching the door. When a server comes up behind him too quickly, he flinches. When a customer raises their voice at the front desk, his hands begin to shake, and he has to step into the walk-in cooler to breathe. He has learned to hide this. He keeps a small piece of ginger in his pocket, and when the panic rises, he presses his thumbnail into it until the pain grounds him.

At home, in his small basement apartment, Rajesh lives alone. He has never dated, never married. He tried once, a few years ago, to go on a date with a woman from his community, but he could not stop scanning the restaurant for threats, and he went home early. He sleeps in short, jagged bursts. He dreams of the concrete room, of the man with the stick, of the sound of boots on gravel. He wakes up with his heart pounding and his fists clenched, and then he lies still in the dark, waiting for the feeling to pass.

He speaks to Priya on the phone every Sunday. She is still in India, still safe, but he cannot shake the feeling that something bad has happened to her. He calls her three times a week, just to hear her voice. She tells him he is being paranoid. He knows she is right, but he cannot stop. He has not been to a doctor. He does not trust institutions. He trusts his knife, his stove, and the rhythm of a busy service. He works double shifts whenever he can. The exhaustion helps him sleep. The heat of the kitchen feels like a kind of safety.

He does not call what he has PTSD. He calls it being careful. He calls it remembering.
